## The challenge

::: lead-para
The **signal-to-noise paradox** in climate forecasting refers to counterintuitive situations where the real world is better predicted than the forecast model suggests.
:::

It arises when predictable mid-latitude atmospheric signals and associated climate impacts are significantly underestimated compared with observations. This discrepancy poses a challenge, as weak signals are statistically problematic to detect, yet underlying dynamical and physical mechanisms, such as remote teleconnections, coupled ocean-atmosphere processes and atmospheric feedbacks, likely play a critical role in the signal-to-noise problem.

## Our ambition

The ambition of AUSPICE is to explain the signal-to-noise paradox by integrating robust statistical methods with physical experimentation and reasoning using causal networks. In order to correct for signal-to-noise errors, the causal networks will be used to calibrate climate predictions and projections, leading to self-consistent, physically grounded climate storylines and more plausible bounds for future climates.

## Project goals

::: goal-grid
::: goal-card
[01]{.num}

### Detect

Apply robust statistical methods to identify where and when predictable signals are underestimated by climate models.
:::

::: goal-card
[02]{.num}

### Explain

Use physical experiments to probe the mechanisms behind the paradox, including remote teleconnections, coupled ocean-atmosphere processes and atmospheric feedbacks.
:::

::: goal-card
[03]{.num}

### Connect

Build causal networks that link these processes to the signal-to-noise errors they generate.
:::

::: goal-card
[04]{.num}

### Calibrate

Use the causal networks to correct climate predictions and projections, producing physically grounded storylines and more plausible bounds for future climates.
:::
:::
